opus-5.5.text:
I think it matters a lot, though maybe not in the way people first assume.

Early on, a lot of founders thought the moat was "we have our own model." I don't think that's where most application companies should spend their energy. Pretraining a frontier model from scratch is enormously expensive, and the base capabilities are improving so fast that whatever you build in-house can be leapfrogged in months.

But being able to *shape* the model, to customize it, fine-tune it, and adapt it to your domain and your data, is hugely important. The gap between a general-purpose model and one tuned to a specific enterprise workflow is often the gap between a cool demo and something that actually runs in production. Things like getting the model to use your company's terminology, follow your compliance constraints, call your internal tools reliably, or reason over your proprietary data are where real value gets created.

So I'd frame it as a spectrum. At one end you're just calling an API with a prompt. That's fine for prototyping, but it's very thin, and your competitors can replicate it overnight. At the other end you're training foundation models, which very few companies should be doing. The sweet spot for most serious application builders is somewhere in the middle. You want a partner, or a setup, where you can get deep access to the model layer. You want to fine-tune, control deployment, and run it privately on your own infrastructure if you need to, especially in regulated industries.

There's also a strategic dimension. If you're entirely dependent on a single closed provider with no ability to influence how the model behaves or where it runs, you've handed a lot of control over your product roadmap to someone else. Their priorities might not be yours. So I think the companies that win will be the ones that treat the model as something they can mold, not just a black box they rent.

r001.rationale: The response says application builders should be able to shape and fine-tune models, while noting that most should not train foundation models from scratch.

r002.rationale: It explains that access to the model layer lets partners customize behavior for their domain, terminology, compliance constraints, internal tools, and proprietary data.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's really important, and I think it's underappreciated right now.

If you look at how most companies are building today, they're taking a model off the shelf, wrapping it in some prompts, maybe doing some retrieval, and calling it a product. That works for a while. But the problem is that you're building on a layer you don't control. The model is the core of the experience, and if you can't touch it, you're fundamentally limited in how differentiated you can be. Everyone else has access to exactly the same thing you do.

Where it gets interesting is when you can actually shape the model to your domain. Enterprises have data that nobody else has. They have knowledge about how their business works, what their customers mean when they say certain things, what a good answer looks like in their context. If all of that has to live in a prompt, you're leaving a lot on the table. Being able to fine-tune, to customize, to actually push that knowledge into the weights, that's where you start to get something that's genuinely yours and genuinely better for your use case than a generic model.

The other piece is control. Companies care a lot about where their data goes, how the model behaves, whether it's going to change out from under them. If you're entirely dependent on an API that someone else controls, you're exposed to all of that. Having some ability to influence or own the model layer gives you stability and lets you make decisions on your own terms.

I don't think every company needs to train a model from scratch. That would be a waste. But I do think the companies that end up winning with this technology will be the ones that treat the model as something they can shape rather than a black box they just consume. The value is going to accrue to whoever can take these general capabilities and make them specific, and that requires being able to reach into the model layer.

r001.rationale: It says companies do not need to train a model from scratch but should be able to shape or customize the model layer.

r002.rationale: It explains how companies can tailor models to their own domains and use cases, but does not communicate that a model provider can accommodate application partners’ specific requirements.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s really important, but I’d distinguish between influencing the model and having to build it yourself. Most companies shouldn’t need to train a foundation model from scratch to build a great product.

What they do need is the ability to adapt the model to their use case. If you’re building something for a particular workflow, you’re going to learn things about where the model succeeds and where it fails that the model provider doesn’t know. You want to be able to take that feedback and improve the system, whether that’s through prompting, retrieval, fine-tuning, or working directly with the provider.

So I think the relationship between the application layer and the model layer needs to be pretty close. If the model is just a fixed black box, you’re constrained by whatever capabilities happen to be available. If you can influence it, you can start optimizing for what your users actually need.

r001.rationale: It says companies need to adapt models to their use cases while most need not train a foundation model from scratch.

r002.rationale: It explains that application-specific feedback can be used to improve the system, including by working directly with the provider, so the model can be optimized for users’ needs.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s hugely important, but that doesn’t mean every company needs to train its own model. It means you need some way to make the model better at the particular thing your users need.

If you’re building a product and you keep running into a failure mode, you want to be able to take examples of that failure and use them to improve the system. Prompting and retrieval give you a lot of control, but sometimes you need to change the model’s behavior more fundamentally. Having access to fine-tuning, or a model provider who will work closely with you, can make a big difference.

The application company has something really valuable: the feedback loop with the user. They know what worked, what didn’t, and what a good answer actually looks like in their context. If that knowledge can flow back into the model, you can build a much better product. If the model is just a fixed API that you have no influence over, you’re leaving a lot of that value on the table.

r001.rationale: It says influence is hugely important while explicitly noting that companies do not all need to train their own model.

r002.rationale: It explains that fine-tuning or close work with a model provider can adapt model behavior to the specific needs of an application’s users.
